SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: Transformer on 2.78 million routine lab values forecasts 162 cancer treatment complications
PUBLISHED: Published 17 November 2026 — npj Digital Medicine, Volume 9, article number 896 (2026), Open Access
SOURCES:
npj Digital Medicine (Lübberstedt J, Braitsch K, Bressem K, et al.) | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03405-8 | primary
FACTS:
- A transformer trained on 2,777,595 laboratory measurements from 3,905 patients with multiple myeloma (1,855) or ovarian cancer (2,050) predicted which of 162 treatment-associated complications would be newly recorded within two years (720 days), across eight clinical categories, "achieving 1.5- to 6.1-fold enrichment above prevalence."
- Across individual endpoints it exceeded non-sequential baselines, including engineered-trajectory models, "by +0.024 to +0.070 in mean AUROC."
- Reported AUROC range across the eight primary disease groups: 0.65 for type 2 diabetes to 0.75 for fungal infections. Inputs were 39 routinely tested analytes plus patient age; 43.1% of analyte-timestep entries were observed, with availability from creatinine 86% / potassium 85% / sodium 84% down to differential counts and platelet indices at ~12%.
- Splits: training P=3,125, validation P=390, held-out test P=390 (1,579 sequences), single tertiary centre, patients treated 2000–2026. External validation on MIMIC-IV and the MMRF CoMMpass registry "showed transferability, strongest for renal and metabolic endpoints, attenuated for infection endpoints"; on CoMMpass it added prognostic value to ISS staging.
- For context the authors note external validation of the CARG/CRASH pre-treatment risk scores "has reported discrimination as low as 0.52 (AUROC) in some populations."
FLAGS: (none)

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: Google-funded WEAR-ME study finds 29.0% of 819 participants have cardio-kidney-metabolic impairment
PUBLISHED: Published 17 November 2026 — npj Digital Medicine, Open Access
SOURCES:
npj Digital Medicine (Esmaeilpour Z, Heydari AA, Metwally AA, et al., Google Research) | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03433-4 | primary
FACTS:
- US cohort (WEAR-ME study, N = 819 participants) integrating continuous wearable data with clinical biomarkers: Chol/HDL, eGFR and HOMA-IR. Funding statement: "This study was funded by Alphabet Inc. and/or a subsidiary thereof ('Alphabet')"; all listed authors are at Google Research, Mountain View, and the acknowledgements thank Fitbit and Pixel Watch study participants and collaborators at Quest Diagnostics.
- Metabolic and cardiovascular disruptions were significantly associated (r = 0.26, p < 0.001), while "early-stage kidney impairment manifests independently."
- Using a normalized deviance score the authors "identified significant health impairments in 29.0% of the cohort": cardiovascular deviation 13.3% (most prevalent singular phenotype), metabolic 9.1%, renal 6.25%, and dual metabolic-cardiovascular impairment in 2.2% of participants.
- Step count, active zone minutes and resting heart rate were identified as the key wearable predictors of cardiovascular and metabolic decline. The authors built a CKM Health Age model they report aligns with metabolic syndrome severity, a modified AHA Life's Essential 8, and user-reported overall health.

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: FDA clears GE HealthCare on-device AI for feeding-tube detection in adults and children
PUBLISHED: November 17, 2026 (Chicago)
SOURCES:
GE HealthCare press release | https://www.gehealthcare.com/en-us/about/newsroom/press-releases/critical-care-suite-3-0-brings-first-on-device-ai-for-feeding-tube-detection-to-x-ray-imaging-in-adult-and-pediatric-care | primary (company)
FDA 510(k) record K253502, "Critical Care Suite with Enteric Tube Positioning AI Algorithm," GE Medical Systems LLC, decision date Apr 14, 2026 | https://fda.innolitics.com/device/K253502 | primary (database mirror; seen via search-result text only)
FACTS:
- GE HealthCare announced FDA 510(k) clearance (K253502) for Critical Care Suite 3.0, AI software that detects feeding tubes on X-ray images and supports assessment of tube placement in adult and pediatric patients; the company says this is the first time the feeding-tube algorithm supports pediatric patients. No age range is given.
- Performance figures in the release: 99.2% sensitivity for tube detection and 91.6% mean DICE localization (described as how closely AI outlines match expert radiologist annotations). The release does not say whether these figures apply to the pediatric population specifically.
- The AI runs on the mobile X-ray device itself and requires no internet or cloud connection; it identifies the enteric tube's path, tip and side port and highlights airways and diaphragm as anatomical reference points.
- Background claims the company cites: mobile X-ray usage of 75% in emergency departments and 51% in ICUs (IMV 2024 report), and about 80% of ICU patients receiving enteral nutrition through nasogastric or nasoenteric tubes (Nikandros et al., 2006 abstract).
- Quotes from Larry Boyd (VP/GM, Global X-ray) and Adam Walbrun (Clinical Manager, Emplify Health, La Crosse, WI), the latter carrying a customer-opinion disclaimer.
- Caveat worth carrying: the matching FDA 510(k) record K253502 shows a decision date of April 14, 2026, so the 17 November item is the announcement, not the clearance decision. I saw the FDA record only through search-result text (auntminnie.com and investing.com both returned 403).
FLAGS: company-claim; update (announcement in window; underlying clearance decision dated April 2026)

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: Lung-ultrasound deep learning reaches AUC 0.95 for TB triage in Kampala prospective study
PUBLISHED: Posted 17 November 2026 — medRxiv preprint, doi 10.64898/2026.11.14.26368125
SOURCES:
medRxiv (Sharma A, Nakiyingi L, … Madabhushi A, Xie YL; corresponding institution Emory University) | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.14.26368125 | primary (preprint)
FACTS:
- Prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025) enrolling people aged 13+ with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary TB, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. Of 318 enrolled, 316 were analysed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis); allocation was training n=223, validation n=20, held-out test n=73.
- One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analysed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network; a 6-zone protocol was derived from training-set attention weights.
- Test-set AUCs: 0.88 (95% CI, 0.80 to 0.95) clinical-only random forest; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) 12-zone ultrasound-only; 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) 12-zone combined; 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models.
- At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 WHO minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity).
- The authors state external validation in intended-use screening populations is needed.
FLAGS: preprint; single-source
(Note: the very wide specificity confidence intervals are quoted exactly as the abstract writes them.)

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: Canadian flu-forecast comparison: AI models beat compartmental model in only four of eight provinces
PUBLISHED: Posted 17 November 2026 — medRxiv preprint, doi 10.64898/2026.11.14.26368122
SOURCES:
medRxiv (Benteke BL, Yusuf W, Cojocaru MG, Champredon D; corresponding institution University of Guelph) | https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.14.26368122 | primary (preprint)
FACTS:
- The study compares XGBoost, LSTM, GRU, Transformer, the Chronos time-series foundation model and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) against ARIMA, Prophet and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM), using weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season. Forecasts were up to 5 weeks ahead, generated per province from October 11, 2025 to March 28, 2026, evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE).
- GRU, Transformer and Chronos achieved lower MAE than the CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan); CEM and ARIMA outperformed all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia) respectively.
- Prophet "always has the highest MAE," and PINN was worse than CEMs. Chronos "performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia," and data-pooling strategies across provinces or viruses "greatly improve deep learning models."
- The authors conclude AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs, but that "these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation," and that AI models are "best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs."

HEADLINE: Osmo claims "human-level olfactory intelligence" for smell foundation model; outside scientists sceptical
PUBLISHED: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 10:20:30 +0000 (MIT Technology Review RSS pubDate)

MIT Technology Review | https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/18/1148816/smell-startup-osmo-ai-nose-good-as-humans/ | report
FACTS:
- Founder Alex Wiltschko claims that in the last few months Osmo's model has achieved "human-level olfactory intelligence," which the company defines as being about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. The company says that last month its model "outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world's largest consumer goods companies."
- Dataset figures per the company: more than 10 million human labels and 800 million "scent tokens"; around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas; before Osmo, fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells existed in databases by Wiltschko's count. Osmo spun out of Google Brain in 2023.
- The Gates Foundation invested $5 million at launch and later gave a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects; Osmo "identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET." Retail fragrances have been created with the technology, including for Procter & Gamble.
- Critic Avery Gilbert (smell scientist, author of *What the Nose Knows*) argued on his Substack in March that some Osmo marketing claims are undocumented and that its patent filings "still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI": "This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI." MIT Technology Review notes a representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.
- Michael Schmuker (former professor of neural computation, University of Hertfordshire, previously an Osmo consultant) says context is central to smell — "[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies" — and that sensor technology will need to improve substantially for medical diagnostics.

  HEADLINE: Experts say EU "MDR 2.0" proposal leaves AI device classification problems unresolved

  SOURCES:
  npj Digital Medicine (Freyer, Cobbaert, Gilbert et al.), Comment, Open Access | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03475-8 | primary

  PUBLISHED: Published 17 November 2026 — npj Digital Medicine, Volume 9, article number 896 (2026), Open Access

  PUBLISHED: November 17, 2026 (Chicago)

  FACTS:

Regulatory News

17 November 2026

by Joanne S. Eglovitch





# FDA to refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ going forward

FDA headquarters in Silver Spring, Md. (credit: Ferdous Al-Faruque)

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced that, as of Monday, it will use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, and policy documents.

The shift was prompted by an executive order (EO) signed by President Donald Trump in September that directs all executive departments and federal agencies to make this change.

The EO only applies only to executive branch agencies and does not affect private industry, Sydney White, an attorney with Wiley Rein LLP, told Focus . This means that pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers will not need to make the terminology change. However, White noted that “private-sector organizations could be affected if any of the EO's directives are enacted into law.”

Christina Silcox, the research director for digital health at the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy, told Focus that “I would consider this more of a semantic change than a meaningful change because neither artificial intelligence nor super intelligence have particularly strong definitions. In both cases, the terms are incredibly broad, and the technical definitions don’t necessarily match up well with common usage, which frequently leads to confusion.”

Silcox expressed concern that using the term “super intelligence” to describe all clinical and clinical-adjacent AI-enabled tasks might lead to an “over-reliance on the results by clinicians and patients.” She emphasized that health systems with effective governance should ensure that users understand what each specific AI tool does, when it should be used, and how to interpret and act on the results.

FDA said the term change will not affect existing guidance documents, regulations, Federal Register notices, and other previously issued FDA documents. The agency said that “where a statute or regulation uses ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’, FDA will continue to quote and cite those terms as written.” FDA also said it will make conforming edits to its public-facing documents “as part of each document’s next substantive revision and updating web content on its regular maintenance cycle.”

According to the EO, the term “AI” is considered outdated. “The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people. Accordingly, the term “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.”

The EO directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST), to provide the President with proposed legislative language that defines “Super Intelligence” within 60 days of the order.

content.content:
**Study design:** "retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework," comparing LLM-generated with clinician-authored discharge summaries.

**Setting and sample:** Admission records from five London hospitals (September 2022 to September 2023), with 1,294 unique cases (649 clinician-authored, 645 LLM-generated), reviewed by 12 resident physicians.

**Model:** "GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI)," used with a clinician-codesigned prompt.

**Primary outcome (adjusted probability of signoff with no or minor edits):**
- LLM-generated: 92.2% (95% CI, 88.2%-94.9%)
- Clinician-authored: 70.0% (95% CI, 56.6%-80.7%)

**Risk difference:** 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0 to 27.5), with LLM minus clinician-authored as the direction.

**Noninferiority margin:** −5 percentage points, prespecified. The lower CI bound exceeded this margin, so noninferiority was met.

**Hallucination rates:** 6.0% of LLM-generated summaries (43 of 720) and 6.9% of clinician-authored summaries (50 of 722).

**Publication date:** November 17, 2026 (JAMA Netw Open, doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.44496).

**Model:** "GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI)," used with a clinician-codesigned prompt.

**Primary outcome (adjusted probability of signoff with no or minor edits):**
- LLM-generated: 92.2% (95% CI, 88.2%-94.9%)
- Clinician-authored: 70.0% (95% CI, 56.6%-80.7%)

**Risk difference:** 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0 to 27.5), with LLM minus clinician-authored as the direction.

**Noninferiority margin:** −5 percentage points, prespecified. The lower CI bound exceeded this margin, so noninferiority was met.

**Hallucination rates:** 6.0% of LLM-generated summaries (43 of 720) and 6.9% of clinician-authored summaries (50 of 722).

**Publication date:** November 17, 2026 (JAMA Netw Open, doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.44496).

+          "bullets": [
+            "RAPS reports the FDA announced that as of Monday it will use \"super intelligence\" instead of \"artificial intelligence\" in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports and policy documents, prompted by an executive order signed in September directing all executive departments and federal agencies to make the change.",
+            "Quoting the order, RAPS reports the government's reasoning: \"The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people. Accordingly, the term 'Super Intelligence' more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.\" The order directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to propose legislative language defining \"Super Intelligence\" within 60 days.",
+            "The change is already propagating through the statistical system. A Bureau of Labor Statistics notice published in the Federal Register on 18 November, seeking OMB approval for American Time Use Survey questions on AI use, states: \"Cognitive testing was conducted using question wording that referred to ``Artificial Intelligence (AI)''. Following Executive Order 14434, terminology was updated to SI.\" The notice lists 7,672 estimated respondents and a 256-hour annual time burden, with comments due by 18 December 2026.",
+            "The order binds executive branch agencies only, so manufacturers need not change terminology, and FDA says existing guidance, regulations and previously issued Federal Register notices are unaffected, with conforming edits made at each document's next substantive revision. Christina Silcox of the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy told RAPS it is \"more of a semantic change than a meaningful change because neither artificial intelligence nor super intelligence have particularly strong definitions\", and warned the label might lead to \"over-reliance on the results by clinicians and patients\"."

+            "The Washington Sun, published 17 November at 7:45 p.m., reports that Wall Street executives and NSA officials told lawmakers the outages \"were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence\", and that the disruptions do not appear to stem from a cyberattack. Three sources familiar with the private conversations said the fixes overwhelmed systems that could not absorb so many changes at once. The account rests on those three sources, speaking anonymously; the NSA \"did not immediately respond to a request for comment\".",

"A congressional official briefed on the matter is quoted: \"These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away.\" Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at Encode, said of legacy software: \"Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won't be a one and done thing.\"",

"Reuters, reporting the same day, says it could not verify the Washington Sun account. "Reuters lists the affected systems as a Microsoft outage disrupting email, a four-and-a-half-hour FAA nationwide ground stop, about 150 United Airlines flights delayed, a JP Morgan Chase software problem, and an Apple outage affecting iCloud and Apple Pay that Apple said was not caused by a cyberattack. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incidents were unrelated and there was \"zero evidence\" they were caused by \"nefarious actors\", adding \"We are not under systemic attack\". No bank or the NSA has confirmed the AI-patching link on the record."

+            "RAPS reports the FDA announced that as of Monday it will use \"super intelligence\" instead of \"artificial intelligence\" in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports and policy documents, prompted by an executive order signed in September directing all executive departments and federal agencies to make the change.",

+            "The change is already propagating through the statistical system. Following Executive Order 14434, terminology was updated to SI.\" The notice lists 7,672 estimated respondents and a 256-hour annual time burden, with comments due by 18 December 2026.",
+            "The order binds executive branch agencies only, so manufacturers need not change terminology, and FDA says existing guidance, regulations and previously issued Federal Register notices are unaffected, with conforming edits made at each document's next substantive revision. entries.name: mcp__Gmail__send_message
entries.description:
FILE REFERENCES: to attach a file you can read here, don't type its base64; set the attachment's content to a file reference, sha256:<64 lowercase hex>:<its absolute path, with / between folders>, and set filename to the file's name. The app fills in the file's content when the call runs. An update_draft call removes a draft's files, so to change a draft that has files, make a new draft with the same files. Sends a new email message immediately from the authenticated user's Gmail account.

To send an existing draft message, provide the `draftId`. To send a new message, provide recipients in `to`, `cc`, or `bcc`, a `subject`, and message content in `body` or `htmlBody` (plain text in `body`, rich HTML in `htmlBody`; do NOT format `body` with Markdown). To thread the message under an existing thread or conversation, provide `replyThreadId` (preferred for send-only clients) or `replyToMessageId`. If sending a new message, attachments can be included via the `attachments` field, but the combined size cannot exceed 25MB. Set `includeSignature` to true to append the user's configured Gmail web signature when sending a new message (ignored if `draftId` is provided).

Returns a Message object with the `id`, `threadId`, and `viewUrl` (if available) fields populated (plus `labelIds` when `draftId` is provided).

Attachment.description: Represents an attachment to be included in an email.

content.description: Required. The base64-encoded content of the attachment.

filename.description: Optional. The name of the file to be attached, e.g. "invoice.pdf". Email clients show this name to recipients for both regular and inline attachments. If not provided, the attachment may be received with no name.

id.description: Optional. Output only. When present, contains the ID of an external attachment that can be retrieved in a separate `GetMessageAttachment` request.

inline.description: Optional. If `true`, this attachment is handled as inline. An inline attachment is content, such as an image, that is displayed within the body of an HTML email instead of being listed as a separate file for download. To display an inline attachment, add an `img` element to `htmlBody` whose `src` is `cid:attN`, where N is the attachment's zero-based position in `attachments`, counting all attachments. For example, if `attachments` contains a PDF followed by an inline PNG, set `src="cid:att1"` on the PNG's `img` element. Don't reference inline attachments by `filename`. Other images in `htmlBody` are removed. If `false` or absent, defaults to `false`, and it's treated as a regular attachment.

mimeType.description: Optional. The field representing a content or media type must use IANA MIME type, https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml. If not provided, defaults to "application/octet-stream".

attachments.description: Optional. The attachments to include in the email. The combined size of attachments in the message cannot exceed 25MB. If you need to send files larger than 25MB, upload the file to Drive first and then insert the Drive link into `body` or `htmlBody`.

bcc.description: Optional. The blind carbon copy recipients of the email. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "[email redacted]").

body.description: Optional. The plain text body content of the email. Do NOT format this field with Markdown (such as headers `#`, bold `**`, bullet points `*`, or tables `|`). If formatted rich text is desired, use `htmlBody` instead. If `htmlBody` is also provided, this field is treated as the plain-text alternative.

cc.description: Optional. The carbon copy recipients of the email. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "[email redacted]").

draftId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of an existing draft to send. If provided, the other fields (`to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `subject`, `body`, `htmlBody`) are ignored, and the specified draft is sent as is.

htmlBody.description: Optional. The HTML content of the email. If provided, this will be used as the rich-text version of the email. Use this field (with valid HTML tags such as `p`, `b`, `ul`, `li`, `h1`) whenever rich text formatting is needed.

includeSignature.description: Optional. Whether to append the user's configured Gmail web signature to the email. Ignored if `draftId` is provided. Defaults to false.

replyThreadId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of the thread to send this message in. If provided, the sent message will be threaded under the specified thread. Compatible with all scopes including send-only (gmail.send).

replyToMessageId.description: Optional. The unique identifier of the message to reply to. If provided, this message will be threaded in reply to the specified message. Note: Resolving a message by ID requires read permissions (e.g., 'gmail.modify' or 'gmail.compose'). If the caller only has send-only permissions ('gmail.send'), use `replyThreadId` instead.

subject.description: Optional. The subject line of the email.

to.description: Optional. The primary recipients of the email. Required if `draftId` is not provided. Each string MUST be a valid plain email address (e.g., "[email redacted]").

Everything landed. Final report:

## Edition 2026-11-18 — published

**Window:** 17 Nov 13:10 → 18 Nov 11:10 UTC (from the previous edition's `generated_at`)

**31 items across all eight sections:** Frontier models & labs (4), Research & papers (5), Security/misuse/threat intel (5), Military/defense/geopolitics (3), Health/science/medicine (3), Policy/regulation/law (4), Compute/chips/infrastructure (5), Deployment & impact (2).

**Lead:** The Washington Sun reported that Wall Street executives and the NSA told Congress this week's US outage wave came from rushing to patch AI-found vulnerabilities — Reuters said it could not verify it, but DNI Jay Clayton attributed the NSA outage to patches for an AI-discovered PHP flaw on the record. It pairs with CISA's same-day Java4Shell alert and OpenAI's own system card rating GPT-6.2 Critical for cybersecurity.

**Storylines filed under** (no new ids coined): `ai-enabled-hacking` ×5, `compute-money` ×4, `china-distillation-export-controls` ×3, `regulating-frontier-ai-us` ×2, `agents-going-wrong` ×1, `ai-weapons-targeting` ×1.

**Validation:** `validate.js --check-links` — 0 errors, 48 links. Three WARNs (JAMA, Forbes, Reuters-via-Yahoo) are bot-blocks on pages I opened and read myself in this session via WebFetch or `scripts/fetch.js`.

**Podcast script: passed.** `validate-script.js` clean (23 blocks, 13 items, 2,298 words). Round one of the adversarial fact-check found 13 instances of drift; I fixed all 13 and round two returned `NO UNSUPPORTED STATEMENTS`. One fix is worth naming: while trimming for the word limit I rewrote a direct quote from the executive order into something the order does not say. I caught it, restored the quote verbatim, and took the words out of unquoted narration instead. One finding — the "fixes overwhelmed systems" mechanism — I resolved by adding the verified sentence to the *edition* rather than cutting it, since it is in the Washington Sun piece I read.

**Sources I could not reach:** `openai.com/index/*` returned 403 to both WebFetch and `scripts/fetch.js`, so GPT-6.2's pricing and the NATO Daybreak figures come from the system card and independent reports, stated as such in the bullets. Reuters, AP and The Guardian are blocked by egress policy (I used the Reuters wire via a syndicating outlet I opened). Also unreachable: Isomorphic Labs' own post, the UK committee's report, and an Oregon DOJ release — each noted in the relevant item.

**Items dropped for lack of verification:** Tencent Hy4 Flash and the Harvard code-review study (both pre-window); OVHcloud Olala and Cerebras (publication hour not confirmed inside the window); two arXiv preprints whose v1 dates conflicted with their listing dates; Microsoft's Maia 300 and Azure infrastructure post (16 Oct, out of window). Benchmark figures for GPT-6.2 that aggregator sites reported but Artificial Analysis does not state — including a widely repeated Intelligence Index score for Astra — were left out.

**Commits:** `9d33a18` (edition) and `82f1a83` (trace), both pushed directly to `main`; remote HEAD matches local. The remote printed a "changes must be made through a pull request" advisory but did not reject either push.

**Email:** sent once to [email redacted], subject and both bodies passed verbatim from the built files, after polling confirmed `https://aiedgebriefing.com/2026-11-18/` returned 200. The edition page and `/script/` are both live.

Nothing failed, so I haven't sent a phone notification on top of the briefing itself — the email is this routine's delivery and it went through.
